choices: GPUs have higher single-thread clock speeds
GPUs offer massive parallel throughput: thousands of cores running the same operation on different data
GPUs have larger per-core caches
GPUs eliminate the need for memory entirely
evidence:
Task: apply the same filter to 50 million pixels
CPU: 8 cores, ~5 hours. GPU: 2048 cores, ~9 minutes.
scenarios.hint: Think about what the 50 million pixels have in common — is each pixel's computation dependent on the others?
scenarios.prompt: Why does the GPU finish 30x faster here?
scenarios.situation: Applying the same image filter to 50 million independent pixels takes 5 hours on an 8-core CPU and 9 minutes on a GPU.
scenarios.title: The 30x speedup
scenarios.why: GPUs are throughput machines: thousands of simpler cores execute the same instruction on different data (SIMT). A pixel filter is embarrassingly parallel — no dependencies between pixels — so it maps perfectly. CPUs optimize single-thread latency with big caches and branch prediction; GPUs optimize total work per second. Match the architecture to the parallelism.

choices: Buy a bigger GPU; hardware solves it
Move the whole pipeline to the GPU including the 2 ms serial step
Profile first: the transfer and the serial step dominate, so batch the work and keep data resident on the GPU
Rewrite everything in assembly
evidence:
Kernel compute: 3 ms
Host-to-device copy: 40 ms
Serial setup: 2 ms (CPU-only)
scenarios.hint: Add up where the 45 ms actually goes — which slice is the compute you wanted to accelerate?
scenarios.prompt: What is the right optimization?
scenarios.situation: A GPU kernel computes in 3 ms, but each run copies 40 ms of data over PCIe plus 2 ms of serial CPU setup.
scenarios.title: The 40-millisecond copy
scenarios.why: The kernel is only 3 of 45 ms — accelerating it further is pointless. The wins are: batch many work items per transfer, and keep data resident on the device across iterations. This is the classic GPU pitfall: PCIe transfer overhead dwarfs compute on small, chatty workloads. Profile before optimizing, always.

choices: Memory-bound: arithmetic intensity is below the ridge point
Compute-bound: the FLOP count dominates
Balanced: it sits exactly on the ridge
Neither: rooflines don't apply to ML
evidence:
Kernel: 0.5 FLOP/byte arithmetic intensity
GPU ridge point: ~8 FLOP/byte
scenarios.hint: The ridge point is where the memory roof meets the compute roof — which side of it is 0.5 FLOP/byte on?
scenarios.prompt: Is this kernel memory-bound or compute-bound?
scenarios.situation: A kernel does 0.5 floating-point operations per byte moved; the GPU's ridge point is around 8 FLOP/byte.
scenarios.title: The roofline read
scenarios.why: Below the ridge point, performance is capped by memory bandwidth — this kernel is memory-bound. More ALUs won't help; the fixes are memory-side: coalesced access, shared-memory tiling, better reuse, or lower precision to move fewer bytes. The roofline tells you which optimization family to shop in.

choices: Registers: slowest, largest
Global memory: fastest per-thread storage
Shared memory: on-chip, shared within a block, much faster than global
Host memory: directly accessible at full speed
evidence: Per-thread: registers. Per-block: ~tens of KB on-chip. Device-wide: GBs of GDDR/HBM.
scenarios.hint: Think about physical distance from the cores: what sits on the chip itself versus out on the memory modules?
scenarios.prompt: Which statement about GPU memory is correct?
scenarios.situation: You are tuning a kernel and need to choose where each data structure lives.
scenarios.title: The memory ladder
scenarios.why: Registers (per-thread, fastest) > shared memory (on-chip, per-block, tens of KB) > global memory (GBs, hundreds of cycles). The art of CUDA is staging data up this ladder: load tiles into shared memory, compute from there, write back once. Every level you climb down costs an order of magnitude in latency.

choices: GPUs always win on total cost
GPUs never win for inference
Compare throughput per dollar including utilization: 4 GPUs at 90% utilization beat 1 GPU at 20%, and idle GPUs are the most expensive kind
Only count the purchase price
evidence:
Option A: 1x GPU node, expected utilization 20%
Option B: 4x GPU node shared across teams, expected utilization 85%
scenarios.hint: A GPU's cost is fixed whether it's busy or idle — so what actually determines cost per unit of work?
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment is cheaper per unit of work?
scenarios.situation: Two quotes: one GPU node at 20% expected utilization, or a shared 4-GPU node at 85% utilization.
scenarios.title: The idle GPU tax
scenarios.why: Cost per unit of work = total cost / utilized work. An idle GPU still depreciates, still draws power, still occupies rack space — utilization is the denominator that matters. Sharing, batching, and autoscaling exist to keep that denominator high. The most expensive GPU is the one sitting idle.

choices: Near-linear: the work splits with minimal communication
Sublinear: PCIe/NVLink and synchronization overhead take a cut
Superlinear: two GPUs are always more than twice as fast
Unchanged: GPUs can't share work
evidence: 1 GPU: 100 min. 2 GPUs: 58 min. 4 GPUs: 36 min.
scenarios.hint: Plot speedup versus GPU count — is each added GPU pulling its full weight?
scenarios.prompt: What does the scaling curve tell you?
scenarios.situation: Training takes 100 min on 1 GPU, 58 on 2, 36 on 4.
scenarios.title: The scaling curve
scenarios.why: Speedups of 1.7x and 2.8x are sublinear — each added GPU contributes less than the last, because gradient synchronization and data movement eat a growing share. This is normal: scaling efficiency is the metric, and it tells you when adding GPUs stops paying. Blindly scaling out is how teams burn budget for single-digit gains.

choices: Threads contain blocks which contain grids
Grids contain blocks which contain threads; a kernel launch specifies both
Blocks and threads are the same thing
Grids run on the CPU, blocks on the GPU
scenarios.hint: Read the launch syntax left to right: what does each number size?
scenarios.prompt: What does myKernel<<<128, 256>>>() launch?
scenarios.situation: You see a CUDA kernel launch written as myKernel<<<128, 256>>>().
scenarios.title: The triple-chevron launch
scenarios.why: A grid of 128 blocks, each with 256 threads: 32,768 threads total. The hierarchy is grid → block → thread, and the <<<blocks, threads>>> syntax sizes the two inner levels. Blocks map to streaming multiprocessors; threads within a block can cooperate via shared memory and synchronization.

choices: 16 threads
24 threads
32 threads
64 threads
evidence: NVIDIA GPUs schedule threads in warps (SIMT execution).
scenarios.hint: This number is the reason shared-memory banks and coalescing are sized the way they are — what is NVIDIA's fundamental scheduling quantum?
scenarios.prompt: How many threads are in a warp?
scenarios.situation: A profiling guide keeps mentioning warps as the unit of scheduling.
scenarios.title: The warp size
scenarios.why: 32 threads per warp — the hardware executes a warp's threads in lockstep. This is why divergence hurts (both branches execute, masked) and why memory coalescing is framed in 32-thread chunks. Nearly every CUDA performance rule traces back to the number 32.

choices: Half the warp takes the if-branch and half the else-branch simultaneously at full speed
Both branches execute serially with threads masked off, so divergent warps take the sum of both paths
Divergence crashes the kernel
The compiler automatically removes the branch
scenarios.hint: SIMT means one instruction for the whole warp at a time — so what must happen when threads want different instructions?
scenarios.prompt: What does this branch cost?
scenarios.situation: Adjacent threads in a warp take different sides of an if/else.
scenarios.title: The divergent warp
scenarios.why: The warp executes the if-path with odd threads masked, then the else-path with even threads masked — paying both. Interleaved divergence like threadIdx.x % 2 is the worst case. The fix is restructuring so threads in a warp agree: branch on blockIdx or warp-aligned conditions instead.

choices: cudaMemcpy with cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost
cudaMalloc
cudaMemcpy with cudaMemcpyHostToDevice
cudaFree
evidence:
float *d_data;  // device pointer, not yet allocated
// need: copy 1M floats from host array h_data to the device
scenarios.hint: Two steps: first reserve device memory, then choose the copy direction — which direction is host-to-device?
scenarios.prompt: Which calls correctly stage the data?
scenarios.situation: You need 1M floats from host array h_data onto the device before launching a kernel.
scenarios.title: The host-to-device copy
scenarios.why: cudaMalloc(&d_data, bytes) reserves device memory, then cudaMemcpy(d_data, h_data, bytes, cudaMemcpyHostToDevice) moves it. The direction flag names source→destination from the caller's view; swapping it is a classic silent-corruption bug. Unified memory can hide this, but explicit copies keep you honest about transfer costs.

choices: Global memory is cached well enough; tiling never helps
Shared memory is too small to matter
Tiling loads sub-matrices into shared memory so each element is read from global once instead of N times
Shared memory only works for 1D arrays
evidence: Naive: each output element reads a full row + column from global memory.
scenarios.hint: Count global reads per element in the naive version versus the tiled version — what changes?
scenarios.prompt: Why does shared-memory tiling speed up matrix multiplication?
scenarios.situation: A naive matmul reads a full row and column from global memory per output element.
scenarios.title: The tiled matmul
scenarios.why: Tiling loads a BLOCK_SIZE × BLOCK_SIZE tile into shared memory once, and all threads in the block reuse it — cutting global reads per element from O(N) to O(N/BLOCK_SIZE). This is the canonical CUDA optimization and the pattern behind fast GEMM: stage data into fast on-chip memory, reuse it heavily, write back once.

choices: Overlap the next batch's host-to-device copy with the current batch's kernel execution using streams
Launch bigger kernels; streams don't help
Use one stream for everything to keep it simple
Copy data after the kernel finishes
evidence: Per batch: copy H2D 20 ms, kernel 25 ms, copy D2H 10 ms. Sequential: 55 ms/batch.
scenarios.hint: Draw the timeline: while the GPU computes batch N, what could the copy engine be doing?
scenarios.prompt: How do streams cut the per-batch time?
scenarios.situation: Each batch copies 20 ms in, computes 25 ms, copies 10 ms out — 55 ms sequential.
scenarios.title: The overlapped pipeline
scenarios.why: With streams, batch N+1's host-to-device copy overlaps batch N's kernel: the pipeline approaches max(20, 25, 10) ≈ 25 ms/batch instead of 55. GPUs have separate copy and compute engines precisely for this. Depth-3 pipelining (copy in, compute, copy out across streams) is the standard pattern for throughput-bound inference and data processing.

choices: Epoch = one batch; iteration = full dataset
Epoch = one full pass over the dataset; iteration = one batch update; batches per epoch = dataset size / batch size
Epoch and iteration are synonyms
Batch size must equal the dataset size
scenarios.hint: How many weight updates happen before the model has seen every image once?
scenarios.prompt: How many iterations are in one epoch?
scenarios.situation: Training on 50,000 images with batch size 100.
scenarios.title: The epoch arithmetic
scenarios.why: One epoch = one full pass = 50,000 / 100 = 500 iterations (weight updates). Mixing these up corrupts learning-rate schedules and logging — 'train for 10 epochs' vs 'train for 10,000 iterations' are very different orders. Get the vocabulary right and every training config becomes readable.

choices: Train longer; the model needs more epochs
Increase the learning rate
The model is overfitting: add regularization, augmentation, or more data — and trust the validation curve, not the training curve
Switch to a bigger model
evidence: Epoch 30: train loss 0.05, val loss 0.42 (was 0.18 at epoch 8).
scenarios.hint: Which curve tells the truth about new data — the one going down or the one going up?
scenarios.prompt: What is happening, and what is the fix?
scenarios.situation: Training loss keeps falling but validation loss bottomed at epoch 8 and now climbs.
scenarios.title: The diverging curves
scenarios.why: Classic overfitting: the model memorizes training data while generalizing worse. The fixes — more data, augmentation, dropout, weight decay, early stopping at epoch 8 — all target the generalization gap. The training curve lies to optimists; the validation curve is the one that matters for production.

choices: The learning rate is too high: the optimizer overshoots the minimum and diverges
The model is too small
The dataset is too clean
GPUs can't train this architecture
evidence: Epoch 1: 2.31, Epoch 2: 2.30, Epoch 3: nan, Epoch 4: nan
scenarios.hint: Loss goes to NaN right after barely moving — what single hyperparameter controls step size?
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
scenarios.situation: Loss: 2.31, 2.30, then NaN, NaN.
scenarios.title: The NaN loss
scenarios.why: A too-large learning rate makes the optimizer leap over the minimum into regions where activations explode to NaN. First move: drop the learning rate 10x and retry — it resolves most NaN-on-epoch-3 mysteries. Gradient clipping and normalization help too, but learning rate is suspect number one.

choices: Train from scratch; pretrained weights bias the model
Use transfer learning: start from a pretrained backbone and fine-tune on your 2,000 images
Collect 2 million images first
Use a larger model from scratch
evidence: Labeled images: 2,000. Classes: 12. Pretrained ResNet available.
scenarios.hint: What did the pretrained model already learn from millions of images that your 2,000 images can't teach?
scenarios.prompt: What is the strongest approach?
scenarios.situation: 2,000 labeled images, 12 classes — far too few to train a deep CNN from scratch.
scenarios.title: The small dataset
scenarios.why: Transfer learning reuses a backbone trained on millions of images (edges, textures, shapes are universal) and fine-tunes the top layers on your 2,000. From-scratch training on 2,000 images just memorizes. This is why pretrained models are the default starting point across vision and language — data efficiency beats architectural novelty.

choices: Convolution looks at the whole image at once
Pooling increases the image resolution
Convolution detects local patterns with shared weights; pooling downsamples for translation invariance and efficiency
CNNs don't work on images
evidence: Model: conv -> relu -> pool -> conv -> relu -> pool -> fc
scenarios.hint: Why slide a small filter across the image instead of connecting every pixel to every neuron?
scenarios.prompt: What do the conv and pool layers each contribute?
scenarios.situation: You are explaining a standard CNN to a teammate.
scenarios.title: The conv-pool pattern
scenarios.why: Convolution applies small learned filters everywhere with shared weights — detecting edges and textures wherever they appear (translation equivariance) with far fewer parameters than dense layers. Pooling downsamples, building translation invariance and cutting compute. This local-connectivity inductive bias is why CNNs dominate vision.

choices: Tune hyperparameters against the test set for the best reported number
Keep a held-out test set touched once at the very end; tune on validation
Skip validation; train on everything
Tune on the training set
scenarios.hint: Each time you look at the test set and adjust, what are you secretly fitting?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct role of each split?
scenarios.situation: You have train/val/test splits and a model to tune.
scenarios.title: The sacred test set
scenarios.why: Train fits weights, validation guides hyperparameters and early stopping, test is touched exactly once for the final unbiased estimate. Tuning against test leaks it into training — your 'test accuracy' becomes a validation number wearing a costume. Methodology this boring is what makes results trustworthy.

choices: It always improves accuracy
It cuts memory ~4x and speeds compute, with small accuracy loss if calibrated well
It only works on CPUs
It increases model size
evidence: FP32 model: 4 GB weights. Target: edge GPU, 1 GB budget.
scenarios.hint: INT8 is one byte versus four — what happens to memory footprint and memory-bound latency?
scenarios.prompt: What does INT8 quantization buy you?
scenarios.situation: A 4 GB FP32 model must fit a 1 GB edge budget.
scenarios.title: The quantization tradeoff
scenarios.why: INT8 stores each weight in 1 byte instead of 4 — ~4x smaller, faster to move (inference is usually memory-bound), with typically 1% or less accuracy loss after calibration. Post-training quantization is often the single biggest inference win per hour of effort. The tradeoff is real but small; the speedup is large.

choices: Process requests strictly one at a time for fairness
Pad every batch to the maximum size
Dynamic batching: accumulate requests for a few ms and run them as one batch
Disable batching to reduce latency
evidence: Triton Inference Server, 50 concurrent clients, p99 latency SLO 200 ms.
scenarios.hint: GPU efficiency loves batches; users hate waiting — how do you serve both?
scenarios.prompt: How should the server handle 50 concurrent clients?
scenarios.situation: Serving with Triton; 50 concurrent clients; p99 latency SLO of 200 ms.
scenarios.title: The batching decision
scenarios.why: Dynamic batching waits a few milliseconds to group incoming requests, then runs one efficient batch — massively better GPU utilization than 50 serial runs, while the small wait keeps p99 under SLO. This is the core latency-throughput tradeoff in serving: pure serial minimizes single-request latency but wastes the GPU; smart batching buys 5–10x throughput for milliseconds of delay.

choices: The KV cache stores past keys/values so each new token attends without recomputing them
It caches the model's weights
It stores training data
It is only useful for CNNs
evidence: Autoregressive generation: token 500 attends to tokens 1-499. Naive: recompute all each step.
scenarios.hint: Each new token needs the keys and values of all previous tokens — do those change as generation continues?
scenarios.prompt: What is the KV cache and why does it matter?
scenarios.situation: Generating token 500 of a long response; naive decoding recomputes attention over all previous tokens every step.
scenarios.title: The KV cache
scenarios.why: Keys and values of past tokens don't change, so caching them turns each decode step from O(n²) recomputation into O(n) incremental work — the difference between usable and unusable long-form generation. The cost is memory: the cache grows with sequence length × layers, which is why long-context serving is a memory game.

choices: It only works for training
Layer fusion, precision calibration (FP16/INT8), and kernel auto-tuning for the target GPU
It makes models bigger for accuracy
It replaces the need for GPUs
evidence: PyTorch model, FP32, latency 85 ms. Target: 20 ms on the same GPU.
scenarios.hint: What if the framework overhead between 200 tiny layers and the FP32 memory traffic are the actual bottlenecks?
scenarios.prompt: How does TensorRT attack the 85 ms?
scenarios.situation: A PyTorch FP32 model runs 85 ms; you need 20 ms on the same GPU.
scenarios.title: The TensorRT pass
scenarios.why: TensorRT fuses layers (one kernel instead of many launches), calibrates to FP16/INT8 (less memory traffic, faster math), and auto-tunes kernels for your exact GPU. The 4x target is realistic because most framework inference is overhead- and memory-bound, not compute-bound. Export, optimize, benchmark — the standard deployment pipeline.

choices: Always minimize single-request latency; throughput follows
Always maximize throughput; latency doesn't matter
Match the metric to the product: interactive chat needs p99 latency, offline batch jobs need throughput
Optimize whichever is easier
evidence: Use case A: chat assistant. Use case B: nightly document processing.
scenarios.hint: A chat user stares at the screen; a nightly job stares at nothing — what does each one feel?
scenarios.prompt: Which optimization target fits each use case?
scenarios.situation: Two deployments: an interactive chat assistant and a nightly batch document processor.
scenarios.title: The two SLOs
scenarios.why: Chat is latency-bound: users feel every 100 ms, so optimize p99 latency (small batches, KV cache, fast interconnect). Nightly jobs are throughput-bound: optimize documents per dollar (big batches, max utilization). Confusing the two is how teams buy latency they don't need or miss latency their users feel.

choices: Profile with Nsight Systems/Compute to find whether you're bound by memory, compute, or launch overhead — then optimize the bottleneck
Rewrite the model in a faster language
Buy a bigger GPU
Increase the batch size blindly
evidence: Inference is 3x slower than expected. No profiling done yet.
scenarios.hint: There are three usual suspects — memory, compute, overhead. How do you identify the culprit before prescribing?
scenarios.prompt: What is the first step?
scenarios.situation: Inference runs 3x slower than expected; no profiling has been done.
scenarios.title: The slow inference
scenarios.why: Profile first with Nsight Systems (timeline: where does time go?) and Nsight Compute (kernel-level: memory vs compute bound?). Guessing wastes weeks: teams rewrite models that were actually bottlenecked on data loading, or buy GPUs for launch-overhead problems. Measurement turns optimization from gambling into engineering.

choices: Generate first, then search for supporting documents
Embed the query, retrieve similar chunks, stuff them into the prompt, generate
Fine-tune on the documents, then generate from memory
Search the web at random and summarize
evidence: 10,000 internal docs. User asks: 'What is our refund policy for enterprise?'
scenarios.hint: The model's knowledge is frozen at training time — where does fresh, company-specific knowledge enter the picture?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct RAG order of operations?
scenarios.situation: Answering questions over 10,000 internal docs the model never saw in training.
scenarios.title: The RAG pipeline
scenarios.why: Embed the query → vector-search the most similar chunks → inject them into the prompt → generate a grounded answer. Retrieval supplies fresh, private knowledge; the prompt constrains the model to use it. This is why RAG beats fine-tuning for fast-changing corpora: updating the index is minutes, retraining is weeks.

choices: One giant chunk per document; simpler is better
One chunk per sentence; maximum granularity
Overlapping chunks of a few hundred tokens, split on semantic boundaries, sized to fit the query's likely scope
Chunks don't matter; the model figures it out
evidence: With whole-doc chunks: retrieved context is 90% irrelevant. With tiny chunks: key facts get split across chunks.
scenarios.hint: Retrieval needs enough context to be meaningful but little enough to be precise — what goes wrong at each extreme?
scenarios.prompt: What chunking strategy works best?
scenarios.situation: Whole-document chunks retrieve 90% irrelevant context; sentence chunks split key facts apart.
scenarios.title: The chunking tradeoff
scenarios.why: Overlapping few-hundred-token chunks on semantic boundaries (paragraphs, sections) balance precision and recall: big enough to contain complete facts, small enough that retrieved context is mostly relevant. Overlap prevents facts from stranding at boundaries. Chunking is unglamorous and decisive — most RAG quality lives here, not in the model.

choices: Cosine similarity between the query embedding and chunk embeddings
Keyword frequency counts
Document age
Random sampling
evidence: Vector database with embeddings for every chunk.
scenarios.hint: Embeddings place similar meanings near each other in vector space — how do you measure 'near'?
scenarios.prompt: How does the retriever rank chunks?
scenarios.situation: A vector database holds embeddings for every chunk; a query arrives.
scenarios.title: The similarity search
scenarios.why: Cosine similarity between the query vector and each chunk vector ranks by semantic closeness — 'refund policy' matches 'money-back terms' even with zero shared words. This is the leap over keyword search: meaning, not tokens. Approximate nearest-neighbor indexes make it fast at millions of vectors.

choices: RAG eliminates hallucinations entirely
RAG grounds answers in retrieved sources, reducing hallucinations — but retrieval can still miss, so cite sources and show uncertainty
Hallucination is not a real problem
Only bigger models reduce hallucination
evidence: Without RAG: 22% of answers contain fabricated policy details. With RAG: 4%.
scenarios.hint: 22% down to 4% is dramatic but not zero — what does the remaining 4% demand of your UX?
scenarios.prompt: What is the honest claim about RAG and hallucination?
scenarios.situation: RAG cut fabricated details from 22% to 4% on policy questions.
scenarios.title: The grounding claim
scenarios.why: Grounding in retrieved sources slashes hallucination because the model quotes rather than invents — but misses still happen (bad retrieval, conflicting sources), so production RAG cites sources and surfaces uncertainty. 'Eliminates hallucinations' is vendor talk; 'reduces dramatically, verify the remainder' is engineering.

choices: The model plans everything perfectly upfront
ReAct loop: reason about the goal, act via a tool, observe the result, repeat
Agents never need tools
One giant prompt with no iteration
evidence: Task: 'Find our Q3 cloud spend and compare to budget.' Needs: query tool, spreadsheet, calculator.
scenarios.hint: No single model call can both look up the spend and do the math — what loop connects thinking to doing?
scenarios.prompt: How should the agent tackle this multi-step task?
scenarios.situation: The agent must query a spend API, read a budget spreadsheet, and compute a comparison.
scenarios.title: The ReAct loop
scenarios.why: Reason ('I need Q3 spend first') → Act (call the spend API) → Observe (result: $412k) → Reason ('now the budget sheet') → ... Each observation updates the plan, so errors self-correct instead of compounding. This loop is the engine of 'Building RAG Agents with LLMs'-style systems: the model thinks, the tools do, the observations steer.

choices: Give the agent one well-described tool per capability: clear name, typed inputs, documented output and failure modes
Give it a single 'do anything' tool
Give it fifty overlapping tools and let it choose
Tools don't need documentation; the model infers
scenarios.hint: The model can only use what it understands — what makes a tool's contract legible to a language model?
scenarios.prompt: What is good tool design for an agent?
scenarios.situation: Designing the toolset for a spend-analysis agent.
scenarios.title: The tool contract
scenarios.why: One crisp tool per capability with a clear name, typed parameters, and documented outputs and errors — the model reasons about contracts, not implementations. 'Do anything' tools produce unpredictable actions; fifty overlapping tools produce choice paralysis. Good tool design is API design with a language model as the client.

choices: Split the model layers across GPUs
Replicate the model on each GPU; each processes different data batches, then gradients are averaged
Split the dataset across CPUs
Use one GPU and hope
evidence: 8 GPUs, 1M images, model fits on a single GPU.
scenarios.hint: The model fits everywhere — so what is there to split?
scenarios.prompt: How should training use the 8 GPUs?
scenarios.situation: 8 GPUs, 1M images, and the model fits comfortably on one GPU.
scenarios.title: The data-parallel split
scenarios.why: Data parallelism: each GPU holds a full model replica, processes a different data shard, and gradients are averaged (all-reduce) each step — near-linear scaling when communication is overlapped. Model parallelism (splitting layers) is for models that don't fit; here it would add complexity for nothing. Match the parallelism to the bottleneck.

choices: Seeds don't matter; GPUs are deterministic anyway
Fix random seeds, version data and code, and log the environment — then you can reproduce any run
Reproducibility is impossible; don't try
Only version the model weights
evidence: 'The good run from Tuesday can't be reproduced. Loss differs run to run.'
scenarios.hint: If you can't name the seed, the data version, and the code commit, what exactly are you trying to reproduce?
scenarios.prompt: What makes training reproducible?
scenarios.situation: Tuesday's great run cannot be reproduced; nobody recorded seeds or versions.
scenarios.title: The unreproducible run
scenarios.why: Fix all randomness sources (Python, NumPy, framework seeds), version the dataset and code, log the container/environment. GPU nondeterminism exists in some ops, but 95% of 'unreproducible' runs are just untracked seeds and data. Reproducibility isn't pedantry — it's the difference between science and anecdote when debugging.

choices: Watch prediction distributions, input drift, and business metrics — with alerts and a rollback plan
Deploy and move on; training metrics guarantee production behavior
Retrain daily regardless of need
Only watch GPU temperature
evidence: Model live 3 months. This week: inputs shifted, conversions dipped.
scenarios.hint: The model didn't change — so what did? And how would you have noticed sooner?
scenarios.prompt: What should production monitoring have caught?
scenarios.situation: Three months live; input distribution shifted; business metrics dipped before anyone looked.
scenarios.title: The silent drift
scenarios.why: Monitor the full stack: input feature distributions (drift), prediction distributions, and the business metric the model serves — with alerts and a one-command rollback. Training metrics describe the past; production data describes the now. Most model 'failures' are data changes wearing a model costume.

choices: Email the weights file to the team
Triton model repository: model_name/config.pbtxt plus versioned subdirectories (1/, 2/) holding the artifacts
A shared network folder with no versions
Paste the model into a wiki
evidence: Deploying resnet50 v1 and v2 for A/B test via Triton Inference Server.
scenarios.hint: Triton needs to know the model's I/O contract and which versions exist — where does it look?
scenarios.prompt: How should the models be laid out for Triton?
scenarios.situation: Deploying two versions of a model to Triton for an A/B test.
scenarios.title: The model repository
scenarios.why: Triton's model repository convention — model_name/config.pbtxt (I/O schema, batching, backend) plus numbered version directories — is what the server scans at startup. Versioning built into the layout makes A/B tests and rollbacks operations, not heroics. Convention over improvisation is the whole MLOps ethos.

choices: Rewrite all pandas code in CUDA C++
RAPIDS cuDF: pandas-like API on the GPU, often with minimal code changes, for the ETL and feature steps
GPUs can't help data prep
Do feature engineering on the CPU and only train on GPU
evidence: Pandas ETL: 45 min. Training: 20 min. Total iteration: 65+ min.
scenarios.hint: ETL is 45 of 65 minutes — which stage should the GPU attack first?
scenarios.prompt: How do you cut the 65-minute iteration?
scenarios.situation: Pandas ETL takes 45 minutes; GPU training takes 20.
scenarios.title: The ETL bottleneck
scenarios.why: Accelerating the 45-minute ETL with RAPIDS cuDF (GPU DataFrames, pandas-like API) attacks the actual bottleneck — Amdahl's law applied to the pipeline. Teams that GPU only the training step optimize the 20 minutes and wonder why iterations still take an hour. Profile the pipeline end to end, then accelerate the biggest slice.

choices: A pipeline: versioned data → training → validation gates → staged deployment with monitoring
Train in a notebook and copy weights to prod
Deploy straight from the researcher's laptop
Skip validation gates to ship faster
evidence: Incident: untested model shipped; no one knows which data trained it.
scenarios.hint: Every production ML incident is a pipeline that didn't exist — what stages would have caught this one?
scenarios.prompt: What pipeline prevents this class of incident?
scenarios.situation: An untested model shipped; nobody can say which data trained it.
scenarios.title: The ML pipeline
scenarios.why: Versioned data → reproducible training → validation gates (metrics must beat the champion) → staged rollout with monitoring. Each stage answers one audit question: what data, what code, what metrics, what changed in prod. Notebooks and laptop deploys work until the first incident — then the missing pipeline is the incident.
